title: My redeemer liveth (Job 19:25)
hook: a flash of hope in the middle of despair

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job turned from his friends and asked for a hearing with God. Your line was I would speak to the almighty. Today, in the middle of that argument, a light comes on.

Chapter nineteen finds Job very low. His brothers are far from him, his friends have forgotten him, his servants treat him like a stranger, and his breath is strange to his own wife. He begs, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Then a wish: "Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! That with an iron pen and lead they were graven in the rock for ever!" Carve it in stone, so somebody, someday, knows what happened to me.
screen: `FORGOTTEN BY FRIENDS.` → `HAVE PITY UPON ME.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Then, suddenly: "But as for me, I know that my Redeemer liveth, and that He will witness at the last upon the dust." From the bottom of the pit, I know. The Hebrew for redeemer is go'el, and it runs through the book of Ruth too: Boaz was the go'el, the kinsman with the right and duty to buy back a family's land and keep a dead man's name alive. In the Torah, a go'el is the relative who buys back what you lost. So Job, forgotten by everyone, says someone will stand up for me. The text doesn't say who, and readers hear it more than one way. Some hear God himself, the God Job is arguing with, somehow also his defender. Some connect it to a line a few chapters earlier, "my Witness is in heaven," and hear a defender on Job's side in the heavenly court. Christians read this verse too, and hear it about Jesus. The lines right after it are hard Hebrew, and translations differ. But the first half stands clear. And notice where it comes: not after his health returns, not after an answer, but in the middle of being forgotten. Hope here isn't the end of the pain. It's a flash inside it. And Job's wish came true in its own way: his words were written in a book, and people still read them.
screen: `MY REDEEMER LIVETH.` · `GO'EL: THE KINSMAN WHO BUYS BACK.` · `GOD, OR A WITNESS IN HEAVEN?` · `HOPE INSIDE THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: If something feels heavy right now, let it be there, and inside it look for one small hope: someone who will stand up for you, a morning you're looking forward to, a belief that holds you. Hold it the way Job held his, not instead of the hard thing but right in the middle of it. If you pray, you can say Job's line, I know that my redeemer liveth.
Go'el. Forgotten by his friends, Job says there is a go'el, a redeemer who will stand up for him, alive. Today's word.
Your line: a flash inside it. Job said I know before anything got better. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish readers study Job 19:25 alongside the go'el, the redeeming kinsman of the Torah and the book of Ruth, and God is called redeemer, go'el, in the Tanakh and in daily Jewish prayer.

A priest who offers sacrifices for you, as Job once did for his children.
A healer who cures sickness, unlike the physicians Job calls of no value.
chat.meaning: In the Torah a go'el is the relative who buys back what you lost; Boaz was one in Ruth. Job says his lives.

Audit: switched Job 19:21–25 and 16:19 from the KJV to JPS 1917 (the path's translation; checked against the 1917 text). The KJV 19:25 'he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth' carries a Christian resurrection reading the JPS 'He will witness at the last upon the dust' does not.
